title.en: A bris of twins on Yesod shebeMalchus

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that by Yesod shebeMalchus the tikkun of Yesod is complete, so a bris on that day signals the child is prepared to be a tzaddik and prepares for Matan Torah; he ties the twins to the mazal of Sivan and closes with brachos.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the week of Emor, the Mashgiach explains why the parsha of the kohanim is the parsha Eliyahu HaNavi will expound, and connects it to Eliyahu at every bris and to a young father who held fast to Yiddishkeit.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach begins with the week's haftorah from Yechezkel about the kohanim, the bnei Tzadok, who kept Hashem's charge when the rest of Yisrael strayed; they kept up the Jewish mesorah, and they will be the ones who draw close to Hashem in the days of Moshiach. The haftorah ends with the prohibition for kohanim to eat neveilah and treifah, and the Gemara asks why kohanim are singled out; Rabbi Yochanan answers that Eliyahu will expound this parsha. The Mashgiach explains that at the geulah the spirit of impurity will be removed and even forbidden things will become kosher, as the Midrash says of the chazir, but the kohanim, as higher Jews, will still not eat them. Every Jew has his own letter in the Torah, and Emor is Eliyahu's parsha. Eliyahu, the kohen tzedek and malach habris, comes to every bris, so a bris in Emor for a young father who fought for Yiddishkeit is a special segulah. He closes with brachos.

en: The kohanim, bnei Tzadok, kept Hashem's charge and the Jewish mesorah when the rest of Yisrael strayed, and they will draw close to Hashem in the days of Moshiach.
Eliyahu will expound the parsha of neveilah and treifah for kohanim because at the geulah even forbidden things will become kosher, yet the kohanim will still not eat them.
Every Jew has his own letter in the Torah, where his learning shines and his chiddushim come, and Emor is Eliyahu's parsha.
A bris in the week of Emor, for a young father who fought for Yiddishkeit, is a special segulah, since Eliyahu, the kohen tzedek and malach habris, comes to every bris.

each jew's letter in the torah

title.en: The bnei Tzadok and the parsha Eliyahu will expound

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the kohanim, bnei Tzadok, who stayed loyal when Yisrael strayed, then brings the Gemara that Eliyahu will expound the prohibition of neveilah and treifah for kohanim, and explains it: at the geulah forbidden things will become kosher, but the kohanim will not eat them.

title.en: Eliyahu's parsha and the bris

summary.en: The Mashgiach teaches that every Jew has a letter in the Torah and that Emor is Eliyahu's parsha; Eliyahu, the kohen tzedek of the bris benching, is the malach habris, so this bris for a young father who fought for Yiddishkeit is a special segulah. He closes with brachos to hear Eliyahu's derasha at the geulah.

catalogTitle: ברית מילה: Bris Milah - Laag Beomer

oneLiner.en: At a bris, the Mashgiach explains that being counted by Moshe Rabbeinu, like being seen by Eliyahu HaNavi at a bris, is itself a great blessing, and that the last, fallen generation of 'Bnei Naftali' is helped from Above when it serves Hashem with mesiras nefesh.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the week's parsha: every tribe is counted 'livnei', with a lamed, except Naftali. He brings the Chasam Sofer: since Naftali was counted last, its number was already known, so its count served only the purpose the Ramban describes, that each Jew came before Moshe and Aharon to be seen and blessed. He then explains why Eliyahu HaNavi comes to every bris: a father who cuts his own child with joy needs help from Above, and Eliyahu, who was moser nefesh for the bris in the episode of Zimri, comes to help. Being seen by him is a great good, like being seen by Moshe. The child is named after Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai. Our generation, the last and 'fallen' one, is Bnei Naftali, and whoever holds on to Torah with mesiras nefesh is helped by Hashem. He closes with blessings.

en: Naftali's count lacks the lamed because, as the last tribe, its number was already known, so it was counted only so that its people would come before Moshe Rabbeinu and be blessed.
Being counted by Moshe and Aharon was a great good for each Jew: Moshe looked at him, asked how he was doing and blessed him.
Eliyahu HaNavi comes to every bris to help the father, who needs great strength and help from Above to cut his own child with joy.
Whoever wants to serve Hashem is helped: angels and souls of tzaddikim come to help him, and above all Hashem Himself.
Our generation, the last one, is 'Bnei Naftali', a fallen generation in which holding on to Torah and mitzvos takes mesiras nefesh, and Hashem helps whoever does so.

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a father who cuts his child with joy needs help from Above, and Eliyahu, who was moser nefesh for the holiness of the bris in the episode of Zimri, comes to help. title.en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, the last generation, and blessings

summary.en: The child is named after Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, and the Mashgiach brings the Midrash Pinchas that the soul whose name is given comes to the bris. He explains that the last generation is Bnei Naftali, a fallen generation, and that whoever holds on to Torah in it with mesiras nefesh receives help from Above, and closes with blessings for the child, the family and all present.

catalogTitle: יש צדיק שמדריגתו למעלה מדורו. ביאור חילוק בין צדיק וטוב לו לצדיק ורע לו.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 10, the Mashgiach explains the difference between the tzaddik who has transformed his evil into good and the tzaddik in whom a hidden residue of evil remains, and describes the special tzaddikim, above their generation, who no longer have a yetzer hara.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens Tanya chapter 10 and says that now the Ba'al HaTanya begins answering the questions of chapter one: what are tzaddik v'tov lo and tzaddik v'ra lo. There are tzaddikim with no yetzer hara, like David HaMelech, whose heart was 'chalal', empty. He describes the special tzaddikim sent close to the days of Moshiach, like the Arizal and the tzaddikim of the Ba'al Shem Tov's era, who remembered earlier gilgulim, and explains why ordinary people forget: to keep their free choice. Pharaoh lost his choice as a punishment, and a story about Czar Nicholas shows that even a rasha's downfall can serve Hashem. The tzaddik who is not complete drives his evil away, but like David leaving Avimelech, it goes off on its own and can return. The complete tzaddik has transformed his evil and despises worldly pleasure, as the Apter Rav did, except where enjoyment itself is the mitzvah, as with eating matzah.

en: There are tzaddikim who have rendered their yetzer hara null and void; David HaMelech said his heart was 'chalal', empty of it, and so he no longer had free choice in that sense.

Close to the days of Moshiach Hashem sends exceptional tzaddikim, above the normal descent of the generations, like the Arizal and the tzaddikim of the Ba'al Shem Tov's era, to keep Klal Yisrael going.
Ordinary people do not remember their earlier gilgulim so that they keep their free choice; perfect tzaddikim, who live only to guide others, may remember.
The tzaddik who is not complete has driven the evil out of the left chamber of the heart, but it was not transformed; a tiny residue remains, subdued and nullified.
The complete tzaddik's evil has been transformed into good, so he despises worldly pleasures that are not for the service of Hashem.
The complete tzaddik hates evil for two reasons: Hashem hates it, and his heart is so filled with love of Hashem that no room is left for any other love.

the yetzer hara of the incomplete tzaddik
love of Hashem and hatred of evil
Kiddush Hashem through the downfall of resha'im

title.en: Tzaddikim with no yetzer hara

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens Tanya chapter 10 and says the Ba'al HaTanya now begins answering the questions of chapter one about tzaddik v'tov lo and tzaddik v'ra lo. He explains that some tzaddikim have no yetzer hara, as David HaMelech said his heart was 'chalal', which means empty, like chillul Shabbos empties Shabbos of its kedushah.

title.en: Exceptional tzaddikim near Moshiach's days

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that although the generations grow smaller, close to Moshiach's days there are tzaddikim beyond the normal descent, like the Arizal, whom Reb Chaim Vital describes as grasping more than the nevi'im. He explains that such people are needed because the state of Klal Yisrael today is so low, and he brings the Ohr HaChaim on falling into the fiftieth gate of impurity.

title.en: Tzaddikim who remembered earlier gilgulim

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the era of the Ba'al Shem Tov, when great neshamos came down and spoke openly of their earlier gilgulim: the Ohev Yisrael of Apt and the Yismach Moshe, who remembered Matan Torah and the dispute of Korach and told his grandson he had stayed neutral. He adds that Korach was a great man with ruach hakodesh, and mentions Reb Shmelke of Nikolsburg and his brother in Mezritch.

title.en: Why we forget: preserving free choice

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that ordinary people do not remember earlier gilgulim because their task is to fight the yetzer hara, and remembering would remove their free choice. Perfect tzaddikim have finished their own task and live only to guide others, so they may remember; he laments that today there is no such leadership.

title.en: Pharaoh, Czar Nicholas and the rasha's purpose

summary.en: In reverse, Pharaoh lost his free choice as a punishment he brought on himself. The Mashgiach tells how a tzaddik explained why Czar Nicholas died a natural death: he was too wicked to merit a Kiddush Hashem through his downfall, whereas Pharaoh did merit it. He brings the passuk that even the rasha was created for the day of evil, and contrasts David HaMelech, who sanctified Hashem with his life.

title.en: The tzaddik in whom evil remains

summary.en: The Mashgiach lays out the four levels the Tanya will explain: the complete and incomplete tzaddik and the complete and incomplete rasha. He reads how a person fights until he drives the evil out of the left chamber of the heart, yet it was not transformed; a tiny subdued residue remains, which is the Gemara's tzaddik v'ra lo, and the tzaddik thinks it is gone. He then asks whether the Ba'al HaTanya uses a passuk merely as poetic language.

title.en: Vayegarshehu vayelech: the evil that leaves by itself

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains melitza, using a passuk out of context, and says the Ba'al HaTanya means every word exactly. He tells how David feigned madness before Avimelech, and points to the extra word in the passuk: Avimelech thought he drove David out, but David left of his own will. So too the incomplete tzaddik thinks he has driven out the yetzer hara, but it left on its own and is ready to attack again.

title.en: The complete tzaddik and the Apter Rav's matzah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that in the complete tzaddik the evil was transformed into good, so he despises worldly pleasures not for the service of Hashem. He tells of the Apter Rav, who could eat an entire goose after a feast, yet at the end of his life said all food tasted like dust to him except the matzah of the Seder night.

title.en: Achila means enjoyment: the body feels the mitzvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach suggests that the mitzvah with matzah is achila, which means enjoying the food, and brings a proof that one must eat it with appetite. He adds that enjoyment leaves a mark on the body: the Gemara holds one who is mis'asek with forbidden fats liable because he had pleasure, and on Pesach the body itself is to be sanctified by feeling the mitzvah.

title.en: Two reasons the tzaddik hates evil

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every desire comes from the sitra achra, and the complete tzaddik hates it for two reasons: Hashem hates it, and his heart is so full of love for Hashem that no room remains for another love, as in 'ohavei Hashem sinu ra'. He raises the question of how one can also love a fellow Jew, and answers that one loves the part of G-d in him, so the love is not divided.

title.en: Tachlis sinah: hatred and revulsion

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings David HaMelech's words that he hates the resha'im with utmost hatred and asks Hashem to search his heart, showing that the measure of his love is the measure of his hatred of evil. He distinguishes mius, revulsion felt toward objects, from sinah, hatred of people, and explains that the tzaddik's soul is revolted by evil as the senses are by spoiled food. He stops at the complete tzaddik.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in Sivan, the Mashgiach distinguishes two brissos, Hashem's covenant of the soul with Avraham and the bris milah that is its sign, and explains that in Sivan, the month of Matan Torah, the covenant between Klal Yisrael and Hashem is strengthened.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with a Midrash that in Megillas Rus every passuk but eight begins with a vav, hinting that Rus accepted the mitzvah of milah. He notes that Avraham received his new name before his milah, though a name is usually given after it. To explain, he distinguishes two brissos: first, Hashem's covenant with Avraham, a bond of the neshamah that ties every Jew to Hashem and does not depend on the flesh, as the Mishnah in Nedarim says that a Jew is called circumcised even if he is not, and a non-Jew uncircumcised even if he is; for this Avraham received his name. Afterwards came the os bris, the bris milah, as a sign of that covenant. A woman shares in the first bris, and that is what Rus took on. A bris in Sivan, when Klal Yisrael came to Sinai and their covenant with Hashem was strengthened, is a great chizuk to feel bound to Hashem, like Avraham, the first of the believers. He closes with brachos.

en: There are two brissos: Hashem's covenant with Avraham, a bond of the neshamah, and the bris milah, which is its sign.
The covenant of the neshamah does not depend on the flesh: a Jew is called circumcised even if he is not, and a non-Jew uncircumcised even if he is.
Avraham received his name for the first covenant, which is why it came before his milah.
A woman also belongs to the covenant of Avraham, and this is what Rus accepted, as hinted by the eight pesukim that do not begin with a vav.
In Sivan, when Yisrael came to Sinai, their covenant with Hashem was strengthened, so a bris in Sivan is a great chizuk to feel bound to Hashem.

title.en: Avraham's name and the covenant of the soul

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that Rus accepted milah, asks why Avraham was named before his milah, and answers with two brissos: a covenant of the neshamah that binds every Jew to Hashem regardless of the flesh, as the Mishnah in Nedarim shows, and the later os bris in the flesh.

title.en: Rus, Sivan and strengthening the covenant

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Rus took on the covenant of Avraham, which a woman shares, and that a bris in Sivan, when Yisrael's covenant with Hashem was strengthened at Sinai, is a chizuk to feel bound to Hashem like Avraham, the first of the believers; he closes with brachos.

oneLiner.en: At a bris on Shavuos the Mashgiach explains, from the end of Megillas Rus, why Oved was given that name: he carried a difficult heritage that he had to refine through hard work, and that is the blessing given to the newborn child.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the blessing in Megillas Rus, 'vayikarei shemo b'Yisrael', which the Targum reads as a wish that the child be counted among the tzaddikim of Israel, and a Midrash that the last eight pesukim of the megillah correspond to the bris on the eighth day. He asks why the megillah repeats the genealogy from Peretz after naming Oved as the grandfather of Dovid. Bringing the Arizal, he explains that Oved carried the soul of Machlon, returned through yibum, and before that the history of Er through Peretz. This is why he was called Oved: the Targum says he served Hashem with a whole heart, but many did that; Oved had to work hard on himself to refine what he was born with. Rus, too, labored all her life on her traits, which is why the neighbors named the child. The Mashgiach ends with the eighth day, above nature, its link to Shavuos, and blessings for the child.

en: The blessing 'vayikarei shemo b'Yisrael' at the end of Megillas Rus is, per the Targum, a wish that the child be among the tzaddikim of Israel, and it was said at Oved's bris.
Oved carried the soul of Machlon, brought back through yibum, and through Peretz also the history of Er, which needed rectifying.
He was called Oved because he had to work hard on himself to refine what he was born with, unlike a tzaddik who serves Hashem easily out of a good heart.
Rus, born a daughter of the king of Moav, labored all her life to refine her traits, and the neighbors named the child because she would not, remembering her past.
Milah on the eighth day is above nature, which runs in sevens, and it is linked to the Torah given as the eighth week begins.

title.en: Oved's bris and the souls of Machlon and Er

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with 'vayikarei shemo b'Yisrael', the Targum's reading of it, and a Midrash tying the megillah's last eight pesukim to the bris on the eighth day. He asks why the genealogy from Peretz is repeated and brings the Arizal that Oved carried the soul of Machlon through yibum, and that Er stood behind Peretz.

title.en: Why he was called Oved

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks, with the Targum that Oved served Hashem with a whole heart, why only he was called by that name. He answers that the histories of Machlon and Peretz merged in him, so he had to work hard on himself, and this made him the forebear of Yishai; milah, too, removes the bad a person is born with.

title.en: Rus, the neighbors' name, and the eighth day

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Rus labored all her life to refine her traits, so she would not name the child, and the neighbors comforted her and blessed him to be an oved. He ties milah on the eighth day, above nature, to the Torah given at Shavuos, and ends with blessings for the child.

oneLiner.en: At a bris on Rosh Chodesh Tamuz the Mashgiach explains that, as milah removes the orlah to reveal the holiness beneath, the dark days of Tamuz hide great light, and contrasts milah, holiness above understanding, with tefillin, the peak of understanding.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach notes that the bris falls on Rosh Chodesh Tamuz, at the start of the period that the navi says will turn into days of joy. Everything in the soul exists in time: the bris kodesh is the greatest holiness, covered by an orlah, and a Jew's work is to remove it; so too Tamuz, the brightest month, is covered, and through toil in Torah and avodah one finds the Shechinah 'bein hametzarim'. Sefer Yetzirah links Tamuz to the letter ches, the first ches in the Torah is choshech, darkness, and Tamuz with its milui equals 'yehi or'. A child circumcised on such a day is suited to reveal that light. From the Gemara on 'sasson' as milah and 'yekar' as tefillin, he explains milah as holiness above daas, given before a child understands, and tefillin as the peak of daas. Everyone at a bris should take this to heart, and he closes with blessings for redemption.

en: Just as the holiness of the bris is covered by an orlah that must be removed, the bright month of Tamuz is covered, and its light is revealed through toil in Torah and avodah.
Tamuz is linked to the letter ches, whose first appearance in the Torah is choshech, darkness; Tamuz with its milui equals 'yehi or', so the darkness turns to light.
A child circumcised on Rosh Chodesh Tamuz is suited to toil in Torah and avodah and to reveal the light of Torah and of Klal Yisrael.
Milah is given to an infant because the holiness of a Jew, rooted in Avraham, is above daas; tefillin, by contrast, is the peak of daas.
Jews have two kinds of holiness: what Hashem gives them, and what they work for themselves, represented by milah and tefillin.

title.en: Tamuz: great light covered like the orlah

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes the bris falls on Rosh Chodesh Tamuz, whose fasts the navi says will become festivals. As the holiness of the bris is covered by an orlah, the brightest month is covered, and through toil in Torah and avodah one finds the Shechinah 'bein hametzarim'.

title.en: The letter ches: turning darkness to light

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Sefer Yetzirah that Tamuz is ruled by the letter ches, the first ches in the Torah being choshech, and shows that Tamuz with its milui equals 'yehi or'. A child circumcised on Rosh Chodesh, which holds the whole month, is suited to reveal the light under the darkness; he blesses the parents.

title.en: Sasson and yekar: milah and tefillin

summary.en: From the Gemara that 'sasson' is milah and 'yekar' is tefillin, the Mashgiach asks why milah is not delayed until the child can do it knowingly, and answers that a Jew's holiness is above daas, while tefillin are the peak of daas. Everyone at a bris should be stirred to bring that root into daas, and he closes with blessings for the geulah.

catalogTitle: צדיק ורע לו - עוד יש לו שייכות אל הרע. “ראיתי בני עליה והמה מועטים” - זה צדיק וטוב לו. ביאור ענין יחוד קובהו"ש.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapters 10 and 11, the Mashgiach explains the levels of tzaddikim, why the highest are called 'bnei aliyah', the meaning of uniting Hashem with the Shechinah, and the many levels of the 'rasha v'tov lo'.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach continues Tanya chapter 10. A tzaddik who never sins but keeps a tiny residue of evil is a 'tzaddik she'eino gamur', and this level divides into countless levels; these are the 18,000 tzaddikim of the Gemara. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's 'bnei aliyah', who are few, transformed their evil into good. The Tanya gives a second reason for the name: they serve only for Hashem's need, not even to quench their own thirst for closeness. The Mashgiach explains 'l'shem yichud': the Shechinah in Klal Yisrael is the kallah, Hashem the chassan, and the tzaddik reunites them. He develops the pattern of mashpia and mekabel in creation, the Sitra Achra's temporary snatching of a destined union, Eretz Yisrael, and David and Bathsheba. Then, in chapter 11, he explains the 'rasha v'tov lo', why a thought of sin can be worse than a sin, and the many levels of this rasha.

en: A tzaddik who never sins but still has a dormant trace of evil is a tzaddik she'eino gamur, and the Mashgiach identifies these with the Gemara's 18,000 tzaddikim.
The 'bnei aliyah' whom Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai called few are those who transformed their evil into good and raised it to holiness.
A second reason for the name is that the bnei aliyah do everything only for Hashem's need, not for themselves, not even to satisfy their own thirst for closeness to Him.
Doing a mitzvah 'l'shem yichud' means uniting the Shechinah dwelling in Klal Yisrael, the kallah, with Hashem, the chassan, and so relieving the Shechinah of its exile.
A 'rasha v'tov lo' is a person whose good is temporarily subordinate to his evil at the moment he sins, but whose strong yetzer tov will bring him to teshuvah.
The rasha v'tov lo has countless levels, from one who slips once in ten years to one who sins several times a day and is full of regret.

title.en: The 18,000 tzaddikim and the few bnei aliyah

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews the tzaddik gamur and the tzaddik who still carries a dormant trace of evil, whose level divides into countless levels. He brings the Gemara's 18,000 tzaddikim and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's statement that the bnei aliyah are few, and resolves them: the 18,000 still have a trace of evil, while Rabbi Shimon had none.

title.en: Turning darkness into light

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the first reason for the name bnei aliyah: they raise and transform their evil into good. He brings the Zohar about Rabbi Chiya, who could not enter Rabbi Shimon's chamber without having turned darkness into light, and notes that the Tanya, which calls itself a book for beinonim, describes this level only so the reader knows what he is not.

title.en: L'shem yichud: uniting chassan and kallah

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the tzaddik who does nothing for himself, not even for Gan Eden or his own attachment to the Shechinah, and explains 'l'shem yichud': the Shechinah in Klal Yisrael is the kallah, Hashem the chassan, and through mitzvos the tzaddik reunites them and relieves the Shechinah of its exile. He reads 'chassid mitchased im kono' as kindness to Hashem's nest, and explains that acting for oneself would mean ego.

title.en: For Hashem's need, not to quench a thirst

summary.en: Reading the Tanya's text, the Mashgiach explains that the bnei aliyah serve for the need above, not to quench their own thirst for Hashem as in the passuk 'Hoy kol tzamei'. He brings the Tikkunei Zohar on the chassid and the Raya Mehemna's parable of a son who gives his life for his parents, then sums up the two explanations of bnei aliyah and notes that the Tanya's bracketed Kabbalistic passage unites them.

title.en: Mashpia and mekabel throughout creation

summary.en: To explain the yichud, the Mashgiach shows that all of creation comes as giver and receiver, sun and moon, day and night, as a parable for Hashem and Knesses Yisrael. The Sitra Achra tries to block this union and at times snatches the kallah away, but only temporarily, like a destined match taken by another, and like Eretz Yisrael, first held by Canaan and then returned to Klal Yisrael.

title.en: David, Bathsheba and the hidden union

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that David and Bathsheba were the destined match of Adam and Chavah and the true parable of Hashem and Knesses Yisrael, from whom Moshiach comes through Shlomo, and that David's desire was spiritual. Asked why it came about in such a roundabout way, he answers that the Satan always tries to block Moshiach's coming, so it is hidden, like a diamond hidden in a garbage can, and he says these pesukim cannot be understood at the surface level.

title.en: Chapter 11: the rasha v'tov lo

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews the levels learned so far and begins chapter 11 on the rasha v'tov lo: at the moment he sins his good is subordinate to the kelipah in the left chamber of the heart, yet he is no complete rasha, since his yetzer tov remains strong. This too divides into countless levels, the lightest being one whose evil overcomes him only rarely and briefly in a small matter.

title.en: Why a thought of sin is worse than a sin

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why thoughts of sin can in a sense be worse than the sin itself: thought reaches far higher than speech and action, so it brings impurity into a higher sphere. He illustrates with a grease spot that is nothing on the street but disgraceful in the king's palace, mentions wasting free time that could be used for Torah, and explains that at the moment of such a lapse the person is a rasha v'tov lo until his good prevails.

title.en: Many levels of the rasha v'tov lo

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes a lower rasha v'tov lo who sins several times a day, like one who learns, davens and gives tzedakah but habitually speaks lashon hara, and brings Chazal that reshaim are full of regret. He stresses that no one is sold to the yetzer hara beyond return, and closes that every person has a deep chamber in the heart that is a tzaddik gamur, which truly means 'l'shem yichud'.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the week of Behaaloscha, the Mashgiach speaks of the kindling of the menorah and explains that while Eliyahu HaNavi's emissaries come to every bris, at a special bris like this one Eliyahu comes himself.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with a theme from Parshas Behaaloscha, the menorah and its daily kindling and preparation. He then turns to the bris itself: Eliyahu HaNavi comes to every bris, but usually it is his emissaries who come, while at a truly special bris Eliyahu comes himself, and he says today's bris is such a one. He speaks of the importance of a bris in a family that has lived through hard times, and closes with blessings that the parents raise the child to Torah and good deeds.

en: The Mashgiach opens with the menorah of Parshas Behaaloscha, its kindling and the preparing of its lamps.
Eliyahu HaNavi comes to every bris, but at most only his emissaries come, while at a very special bris he comes himself.
The Mashgiach says that today's bris is such a bris, to which Eliyahu comes himself.
A bris in a family that has gone through hard times is an especially precious bris.

title.en: The menorah, and Eliyahu at a special bris

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the menorah of Behaaloscha, then explains that Eliyahu's emissaries come to every bris but Eliyahu himself comes to a special bris, as he says today's is. He speaks of the worth of a bris in a family that has known hardship and closes with blessings for the child and parents.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the week of Behaaloscha, the Mashgiach explains Rashi's praise that Aharon 'did not change': he chose the lamps, which bring Torah and sons who are talmidei chachamim, over the ketores, which brings wealth, every day for forty years, and wishes that this home merit both together.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Rashi on 'vaya'as ken Aharon' in this week's parsha: it tells Aharon's praise, that he did not change. He explains that in the Beis HaMikdash the one who merited to offer the ketores had a promise of wealth, while the avodah of preparing the lamps brought the merit of Torah and of sons who are talmidei chachamim. Aharon, who could pick any avodah he wished, took the lamps every day, and since one person cannot do both, he gave up the ketores. The Mashgiach asks why, in forty years in the desert, Aharon did not give up the lamps even one day to gain a little wealth, as a father needs to marry off children, and answers that this is his praise: he never changed. He then turns to the bris, where Torah is precious in the family, and blesses the father, the grandparents and the guests that the light of Torah shine from the home, together with greatness.

en: Rashi's words on 'vaya'as ken Aharon', that he did not change, are Aharon's praise for lighting the lamps every day.
The Mashgiach says that offering the ketores carried a promise of wealth, while the avodah of the lamps brought Torah and sons who are talmidei chachamim.
Since one person cannot both prepare the lamps and offer the ketores, Aharon's daily choice of the lamps meant giving up the ketores.
The Mashgiach applies this to the bris: in this family Torah is precious, and he wishes that the light of Torah shine from the home.

title.en: Aharon chose the lamps over the ketores

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains Rashi's praise of Aharon that he did not change: he took the lamps, which bring Torah and sons who are talmidei chachamim, and gave up the ketores, which brings wealth, every day for forty years. He applies it to the family of the bris and closes with blessings for the father, the grandparents and the guests.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the week of Parshas Balak, the Mashgiach explains that the parsha is named for the hidden spark of Moshiach in Balak, that the days of bein hametzarim hold great kedusha covered by an orlah, and that a bris now is a sign that Hashem will remove that orlah and bring the geulah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach asks why a parsha should be named after Balak. He explains that Balak usually falls just before the three weeks, and the holy sefarim say these days will become the greatest days, as Zechariah says the fasts will turn to joy; now they are covered by din. Where kedusha is greatest the kelipah is strongest, as the Sfas Emes says, in a person, in a place such as Eretz Yisrael, and in time. Hashem will come as the mohel and remove this orlah. Balak, a terrible kelipah, held a holy spark, for Chazal say he was the ancestor of Rus and so of Moshiach ben David; the parsha is named for that spark. Balak feared that the orlah would be removed and Moshiach revealed, but in the end the spark came out. A bris in this week is therefore a good sign, and the Mashgiach says that at such a bris Eliyahu HaNavi himself comes, and he blesses the family.

en: The days of bein hametzarim are destined to be the greatest days of the year, but now they are covered by din.
Where kedusha is greatest, the kelipah over it is strongest, and it must be cut away.
The parsha is named after Balak because of the holy spark in him, from which Moshiach ben David descends.
A bris in Parshas Balak is a good sign that Hashem will remove the orlah of these days and reveal their kedusha.
Eliyahu HaNavi, the herald of the geulah, comes to every bris, and to an important bris he comes himself.

title.en: Great kedusha covered by an orlah

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why a parsha is named after Balak, and explains that the coming days of bein hametzarim hold the greatest kedusha, now covered by din, because where kedusha is greatest the kelipah is strongest, in a person, a place and a time. Hashem will come as the mohel and remove the orlah.

title.en: Balak's hidden spark and the bris

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Balak held a spark of Moshiach, as the ancestor of Rus, and feared its revelation, yet it came out in the end; a bris in this week is a good sign of the geulah. He adds that Eliyahu HaNavi himself comes to an important bris and closes with blessings for the family.

catalogTitle: רשע וטוב לו - יש לו חרטה אחר העבירות אבל לא עשה תשובה. רשע ורע לו - נשמות שמסר יעקב לעשו - אבל יש להם נקודת יחידה ומצטרפים למנין.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 11, the Mashgiach explains the rasha who still feels regret and the rasha in whom the good has departed, and shows that even the lowest Jew keeps a surrounding holiness that joins him to a minyan and that Purim, especially in Adar Sheni, celebrates.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach continues Tanya chapter 11. A rasha v'tov lo sins often, yet the living good in him brings thoughts of regret between his sins, though he lacks the strength to stop; the Slonimer Rebbe's mashal of the drunkard who rewarded his three sober days with a drink illustrates him. The rasha v'ra lo never thinks of teshuvah; these are the souls Yaakov sent to Esav, and the Midrash of the am ha'aretz shows they will return to Yaakov when Moshiach comes. The good in such a person has left its nest but hovers above him as a makif. In a long Purim digression the Mashgiach explains, through Amalek, the tribe of Dan, Haman's silver and the silver hooks of the Mishkan, that Hashem never rejects the Jews outside the camp. He then explains that this makif of Yechidah is why ten reshaim make a minyan, and closes with Adar Sheni, Shushan Purim in Yerushalayim, and questions from the listeners.

en: A rasha v'tov lo still has a living good inclination that brings regret between his sins, but it lacks the strength to make him abandon them.
A rasha v'ra lo never thinks of teshuvah; he is the counterpart of the tzaddik who never thinks of sinning.
The good that leaves such a person does not abandon him altogether but hovers above him as a makif, a surrounding light, like a bird hovering over its nest.

Above every Jew is a holiness of Yechidah, the fusion of all the souls of Klal Yisrael, that no sin can touch; it is revealed when ten Jews gather, which is why ten reshaim make a minyan and nine tzaddikim do not.
Hashem never rejects the Jews whom Amalek and Haman regarded as outcasts, and this is the special joy of Purim, especially in Adar Sheni.

candidateTopics: rasha v'tov lo and rasha v'ra lo
no Jew is rejected by Hashem

title.en: The rasha who still feels regret

summary.en: After finding the place in Tanya chapter 11, the Mashgiach explains that a momentary sinner is a rasha only at that moment, and then describes the rasha v'tov lo who sins often and harshly, yet has thoughts of teshuvah between his sins from the living good in him, without the strength to stop.

title.en: The Slonimer Rebbe's mashal of the drunkard

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Slonimer Rebbe's reading of the passuk 'mi yiten tahor mitamei lo echad' with the mashal of a drunkard who stayed sober three days and then rewarded himself with a drink, and applies it to the rasha who has regret but not the strength of a firm 'no'.

title.en: The souls Yaakov sent to Esav

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that those ruled by the yetzer hara are the souls Yaakov sent to Esav, and tells the Midrash of an am ha'aretz who taught Rabbi Hoshaya that Esav's kings will return the gift to Moshiach; he explains that this was the am ha'aretz's own portion in the Torah, that these souls will return to Yaakov.

title.en: The rasha v'ra lo and the hovering good

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya's description of the rasha v'ra lo, who never has thoughts of teshuvah because the good has left its place in his heart, and explains that it still hovers above him as a makif, like a bird above a nest occupied by a serpent, comparing it to the tzelem Elokim that hovers above a non-Jew.

title.en: Adar, the tribe of Dan and Amalek

summary.en: Turning to the month of Adar, the Mashgiach explains that Adar at the end of the year corresponds to the lowest souls, and recalls that the idol-carrying Jews of the camp of Dan were expelled from the Clouds of Glory and fell to Amalek; Hashem does not forgive Amalek for having no mercy on them, because no Jew is rejected by Him.

title.en: Haman's silver and the hooks of the Mishkan

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Haman's ten thousand talents were meant to cancel the half-shekel of the six hundred thousand, but he did not redeem the surplus that became the silver hooks outside the holiness of the Mishkan, the portion of the rejected Jews; this was the 'parashas hakesef' Mordechai told Esther. He adds that the thirteenth month, Adar Sheni, lies outside the twelve combinations of Hashem's Name, and the Purim miracle happened in it.

title.en: Yechidah and the minyan of ten reshaim

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why ten reshaim make a minyan while nine tzaddikim cannot, and answers that above every Jew hovers a level of the soul, Kedushas Yisrael or Yechidah, the fusion of all souls in the soul of Yaakov Avinu, that no sin affects; Korach's flaw reached up to Levi but not to Yisrael, and ten Jews together reveal this makif.

title.en: The end of the perek and the Purim of Yerushalayim

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the last lines of the perek, that even the worst rasha has the makif above him and therefore Chazal say the Shechinah rests on every ten Jews, and returns to the joy of Adar Sheni; he explains that Purim is for the rasha who still has regret, and Shushan Purim of Yerushalayim, a walled city, is for those who have nothing but the makif.

title.en: Questions: the inner point, sukkah and the minyan

summary.en: Answering listeners, the Mashgiach explains that the point in every Jew is truly his, but it comes to expression only as a makif when he davens with a minyan; he compares the makif to the sukkah and says it can become inner on Simchas Torah. He adds that one guards against the contagion of rishus but must still care for the rasha, and that the minyan is learned from Korach's congregation.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the nine days, the Mashgiach explains that the bris removes the orlah that covers kedusha, in a person, in a place and in time, and that the mourning set aside for a bris in these days is a sign that Hashem will remove the orlah of churban and reveal their greatness.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach asks what connection a bris has to the customs of the nine days, which are set aside for it: the participants may eat meat, drink wine and take a haircut. He explains that a bris removes the orlah from the holy covenant and reveals the kedusha of the Jewish child, and that, following Sefer Yetzirah, there is orlah in a person, in a place and in time. Eretz Yisrael and Yerushalayim, the place of the Mikdash and the Shechinah, are now covered by an orlah made by the galus, which Moshiach will remove. These days too, which the holy sefarim call great days and which Zechariah says will turn to joy, are covered by the orlah of churban. A bris in the nine days, when the mourning is lifted, is therefore a sign that the orlah of the time will be removed, and he blesses that Eliyahu HaNavi come and bring the geulah.

en: The bris sets aside the mourning customs of the nine days: meat, wine and haircuts are permitted to those taking part.
A bris removes the orlah and reveals the kedusha that is covered in a Jewish child.
Orlah exists in three dimensions, in a person, in a place and in time.
Eretz Yisrael, the place of the Mikdash, is now covered by an orlah made by the galus, which Moshiach will remove to reveal the Shechinah.
The days of the three weeks are destined to be great days, but are now covered by the orlah of churban.

bein hametzarim as days of future joy

title.en: Orlah over a child and over the land

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why a bris sets aside the customs of the nine days, and explains that a bris removes the orlah from a child's kedusha. Orlah exists in a person, a place and time; Eretz Yisrael, the place of the Mikdash, is now covered by the orlah of galus.

title.en: The orlah of the time and the bris

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that these days are destined to be great days, as Zechariah says, but are covered by the orlah of churban; a bris now, when the mourning is lifted, is a sign that Hashem will remove that orlah. He closes with blessings that Eliyahu HaNavi come and bring the geulah.

oneLiner.en: At a bris seudah, the Mashgiach explains that while every generation, year and moment has its own task, the bris is the eternal covenant that carries Yiddishkeit and emunah unchanged from one generation to the next.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with 'to pass into the covenant' from Parshas Nitzavim and explains that a bris is something made eternal. He brings Rashi in Parshas Noach that a covenant was needed so the fruits would not spoil. Every generation, year and moment has its own conduct and task, to be fulfilled in its time, yet beneath the change runs the eternity of Klal Yisroel: to be Hashem's chosen people, do His will and crown Him King over the world. Names change with each mission, as Rashi says, but this never changes. Milah, unlike other mitzvos, hands emunah from one generation to the next, a covenant made even with the unborn. Amalek, who scorned milah, fights this eternity, so Hashem's war with him lasts from generation to generation. The Mashgiach closes with blessings.

en: A bris is something made eternal: like the covenant over the fruits in Noach's ark, it is what keeps a thing from spoiling.
Every generation, year and moment has its own conduct and its own task that must be fulfilled at that time.
Beneath every change there is an eternity of Klal Yisroel that never changes, and this is the meaning of the bris.
The Jewish people's task, to be Hashem's chosen people, do His will and crown Him King over the whole world, does not change from day to day, year to year or generation to generation.
Milah differs from other mitzvos: it is the handing down of emunah and Yiddishkeit from one generation to the next.
Amalek, who scorned milah, is the force that opposes the eternity of Klal Yisroel, and so Hashem's war with him is from generation to generation.

title.en: The bris as what makes things eternal

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with 'to pass into the covenant' from Parshas Nitzavim and Rashi in Parshas Noach on the covenant over the fruits, and explains that a bris preserves. He contrasts this with the changing conduct of every generation, year and moment, beneath which runs the eternity of Klal Yisroel.

title.en: Milah: handing emunah to the next generation

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Jewish people's role toward Hashem never changes, though names change with each mission, and that milah, unlike other mitzvos, carries emunah from generation to generation, a covenant made even with the unborn. He then explains Amalek, who scorned milah, as the force opposing this eternity, hence the war 'from generation to generation'.

title.en: The father's mesirus nefesh and blessings

summary.en: The Mashgiach praises the father's mesirus nefesh for emunah and Yiddishkeit, says this gives an assurance that Amalek will have no hold here, and that today's bris is made with the generations to come. He closes with blessings that Yiddishkeit continue in the family and that Hashem's kingship be revealed over the whole world.

oneLiner.en: At a bris, the Mashgiach explains why the Harachaman for Moshiach mentions the 'chasan damim' of Moshe Rabbeinu's son, and why a bris in a time of weakened milah is a harbinger of the geulah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Harachaman prayers said at a bris and asks why the one for Moshiach is tied to the merit of 'chasan damim lamulos', the milah of Moshe Rabbeinu's son, and why it speaks of good tidings. He asks how Moshe Rabbeinu could have delayed his son's milah, and compares it to the Midrash on the breaking of the luchos: Moshe did not want to be separated from klal Yisroel. Using the Ibn Ezra that milah is a sign by which Jews recognize one another, he explains that the punishment of kareis for not doing milah, like that for eating on Yom Kippur, comes from cutting oneself off from the community. In Egypt the Jews had stopped doing milah, and Moshe, pained by this, held back his own son's milah to arouse mercy above for all of them. Today too milah has been weakened among millions of Jews, so a bris now is a sign that the geulah is near. He closes with blessings for the family.

en: The Mashgiach asks why the Harachaman for Moshiach is said in the merit of 'chasan damim lamulos', when Moshiach should come in his own merit.
Following the Ibn Ezra, the Mashgiach says milah is a sign by which Jews everywhere recognize one another as Jews.
The kareis for not doing milah, like the kareis for eating on Yom Kippur, is explained as the result of separating oneself from klal Yisroel.
Moshe Rabbeinu held back his son's milah because the Jews in Egypt were not circumcising, in order to arouse mercy above for them.
In our time, as before the Exodus, milah has been weakened among millions of Jews, so a bris now is a good sign that the geulah is coming.

candidateTopics: milah as a sign of Jewish identity
kareis and separation from the community

title.en: Harachaman, Moshiach and 'chasan damim'

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Harachaman for Moshiach at a bris mentions the merit of 'chasan damim lamulos' and good tidings. He then asks how Moshe Rabbeinu could have delayed his son's milah, and points to the Midrash that Moshe broke the luchos because he did not want to be separate from klal Yisroel.

title.en: Milah as the sign of belonging to klal Yisroel

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ibn Ezra that milah is a sign by which Jews recognize each other, and a sefer's explanation that kareis for eating on Yom Kippur comes from separating from the community; the same applies to milah. Since in Egypt the Jews had stopped doing milah, Moshe Rabbeinu held back his own son's milah to arouse mercy above, which is why it says 'lamulos' in the plural.

title.en: A bris today as a harbinger of the geulah

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares our time, before the geulah, to the time before the Exodus: milah has been weakened among millions of Jews in Russia, America and everywhere. Since Moshe Rabbeinu is connected to Moshiach, a bris in the week of the parsha of bris milah is a good sign of redemption; he ends with blessings for the father, the family and all present.

catalogTitle: האדם נברא ביכולת שישליט המוח על הלב. יש לכל יהודי שורש הנעלם שכולו טוב. שייכות לפורים.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 12, the Mashgiach explains that the beinoni's evil is only subdued, not killed: it is silenced during true davening and wakes again afterward, yet his mind always has the power to rule over his heart.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens Tanya chapter 12 and explains that the beinoni, whose evil never overpowers the good, is what we would call a tzaddik, yet he keeps the potential to sin. Comparing it to the Rambam's testimony of the One Who knows hidden things about a baal teshuvah, he says the term describes a present, resolute condition. An antibiotics analogy shows the difference: the tzaddik killed his yetzer hara, the beinoni only knocked it out. He explains the three judges and why the beinoni still gets full credit. During davening, when a channel is cut upward through Pesukei Dezimra and the brachos of Krias Shema, the beinoni rises like a tzaddik; afterward he falls back, like a dancer landing. Finally, an undesirable thought is no failing but a chance for the mitzvah of not straying after the heart, since the mind was created to rule the heart.

en: The beinoni of Tanya never sins and would seem a tzaddik to us, but his yetzer hara is still alive within him.
Being a beinoni describes a present resolute state, so a later sin does not mean he never was one, and teshuvah restores it.
The tzaddik has killed his yetzer hara, while the beinoni has only knocked it out, so it may revive.
During true davening the beinoni's evil is rendered powerless and he is like a tzaddik, but after davening it awakens again.
Pesukei Dezimra cut a channel up through the obstructions, and the brachos of Krias Shema bring down yiras Shamayim and ahavah.
An undesirable thought is not a failing but a chance for the mitzvah of not straying after one's heart; the sin is only letting it linger.
Every person was created with a mind that can rule his heart, so there is no excuse to say he cannot control his thoughts.

title.en: Who is the beinoni of chapter 12

summary.en: After greeting a new listener, the Mashgiach opens chapter 12 on the beinoni, whose evil never overpowers the good, and explains that we would call him a tzaddik. The real tzaddik, like Dovid HaMelech, has killed the yetzer hara in the left chamber of his heart and replaced it with good.

title.en: A present state, like the Rambam's teshuvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the beinoni's yetzer hara is suppressed but still there, and that being a beinoni describes his present resolute condition, as the Rambam says of a baal teshuvah that the One Who knows hidden things testifies about him. An analogy of antibiotics taken for too short a time shows the difference between knocking out the yetzer hara and killing it.

title.en: Rasha, tzaddik v'ra lo and the three judges

summary.en: Answering a listener, the Mashgiach distinguishes the rasha and the tzaddik v'ra lo from the beinoni, then explains the judges: the yetzer hara judges the rasha, the yetzer tov the tzaddik, and both the beinoni. Hashem helps the beinoni, and with the passuk 'Hashem lo ya'azvenu' he explains that at the judgment he still gets full credit.

title.en: No barrier: the beinoni's davening

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that sins create a barrier between a person and his neshamah, so his thoughts wander in davening; he brings the Ba'al Shem Tov that every word of tefillah is a heichal from which the unworthy are thrown out. The beinoni has no such barrier, so while davening he feels the malachim singing and has the status of a tzaddik.

title.en: A person is where his thought is

summary.en: On the Tanya's 'special times' of davening, the Mashgiach brings the Ba'al Shem Tov that a person is where his thought is, proves it from the halachah of designating a tree as one's Shabbos resting place, which he saw in the Satmar Rav and the Avnei Nezer, and applies it to having Yerushalayim in mind in davening.

title.en: The eis ratzon that moves with the sunrise

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how an eis ratzon outside Eretz Yisrael can be real when everything follows Eretz Yisrael, noting that the Ramak says those abroad miss out and the Ba'al HaTanya in his Shulchan Aruch disagrees. He explains that Above there is no time, and the eis ratzon formed at sunrise moves along with the sunrise, which is why Shacharis is the main time and needs a long davening with tallis and tefillin.

title.en: Cutting a channel: the order of davening

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the air up to Shamayim is full of klipos from people's sins, and Pesukei Dezimra cut a channel through them, as the Arizal reads 'zimra' as cutting. Then the brachos of Krias Shema bring down yiras Shamayim and ahavah, preparing for Shema itself, and the bracha after Shema extends yetzias Mitzrayim, freeing oneself from everything that keeps him from Hashem.

title.en: Rising in davening, falling back after

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that during genuine davening the beinoni's evil becomes subservient to the good and powerless, since even the body sees its root, as the chayos rise to the level of the serafim. After davening the motor shuts off and he falls back, like Chassidim who dance and rise off the ground only for a moment; the evil wakes again but remains only one judge.

title.en: Undesirable thoughts and 'machshavah mamash'

summary.en: The Mashgiach teaches that an undesirable thought comes from the yetzer hara, not from the person's essence, and is no reason to feel guilty; it is an opportunity for the mitzvah of 'v'lo sasuru', which is transgressed only by letting the thought linger. He explains that the beinoni never lets in a 'machshavah mamash', a fully developed thought.

title.en: The mind rules the heart; Reb Shmelke's dveikus

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the mind is the ruler over the heart and every person was created able to hold himself back. He tells of the Rebbe Reb Shmelke, who asked his students to tap him if he lost his dveikus while learning, and explains that Torah learned with dveikus is like tefillah, but the Tanya speaks of tefillah. He ends answering a question about Pesukei Dezimra and the eis ratzon.

oneLiner.en: At a bris, the Mashgiach links the father's eight days of involvement in his son's milah to the Jew whose heart is always in Yerushalayim, and blesses him to merit seeing the Shechinah three times a year.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Harachaman of the bris that links the milah on the eighth day to going up to see the Shechinah three times a year. He explains that a Jew longs all year for the time he can go to Yerushalayim for Yom Tov, and as the passuk says of the Beis HaMikdash, 'My eyes and My heart shall be there all the days': since his thoughts are there, it is as if he is there constantly. He then brings Tosafos' question why a passuk is needed to exempt a woman from milah, and an answer in the Rishonim: the father is bound by the mitzvah day and night for all eight days, since he must arrange that the bris be on time. Today, when problems with a bris on the eighth day are common and a father runs between doctor and rav, he is busy with the mitzvah all eight days; measure for measure, the Mashgiach blesses him to go up to Yerushalayim and see the Shechinah.

en: A Jew who longs all year for Yerushalayim has his heart there constantly, so it is as if he is always there.
According to an answer in the Rishonim, milah is not a time-bound mitzvah for the father, since he is obligated day and night for all eight days to make sure the bris happens on time.

When a father runs between doctor and rav for eight days and nights to arrange the bris, he is busy with the mitzvah the whole time, and measure for measure should merit going up to see the Shechinah.

title.en: Eight days of milah and the longing for Yerushalayim

summary.en: The Mashgiach connects the Harachaman's blessing to see the Shechinah three times a year with the eight days of milah. He explains that a Jew whose heart is always in Yerushalayim is as if there constantly, brings an answer in the Rishonim that the father is bound by the mitzvah all eight days, and applies it to a father who ran between doctor and rav to arrange the bris.
